content: The tuberculosis (TB) incidence rate in 2008 was the lowest recorded since national reporting began in 1953, with only 2 cases per 100,000 population. This report provides a detailed analysis of provisional 2008 data from the National TB Surveillance System and examines trends since 1993. It highlights that foreign-born individuals and racial/ethnic minorities continue to bear a disproportionate burden of TB in the United States. Specifically, TB rates among Hispanics and Blacks were nearly eight times higher than those among non-Hispanic Whites, while rates among Asians were approximately 23 times higher. In 2008, among individuals with known country of origin, 95% of Asians, 76% of Hispanics, 32% of Blacks, and 18% of Whites with TB were foreign-born. Health departments across all 50 states and the District of Columbia electronically report verified TB cases to the CDC, adhering to the CDC/Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists case definition. These reports include demographic data (e.g., race/ethnicity), treatment information, and, when available, drug-susceptibility test results. The national TB rate and percentage change from 2007 to 2008 were calculated using U.S. Census population estimates. The proportion of TB cases contributed by foreign-born individuals has increased annually since 1993. To address this, the CDC issued revised technical instructions in 2007 for TB screening and treatment among individuals applying for immigration to the United States. These instructions include culture and drug-susceptibility testing for suspected TB cases, administration of directly observed therapy (DOT) overseas before entry, and targeted tuberculin skin testing for children from high-incidence countries and contacts of known TB cases. Despite progress, multidrug-resistant TB (MDR TB) remains a significant challenge, disproportionately affecting foreign-born individuals in the U.S. Approximately 1% of culture-positive TB cases have been MDR TB since 1997. The CDC continues to provide technical assistance to domestic and international partners to enhance MDR TB detection and improve access to second-line TB drugs. In Chuuk, part of the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), TB is endemic, with 70 cases recorded in 2007. Limited transportation and healthcare infrastructure hinder access to diagnostic services, such as chest radiography and smear microscopy. Routine culture confirmation, drug-susceptibility testing, and genotyping only became available in FSM in 2006 through referral laboratories in Hawaii and California. Before 2008, active case-finding and administration of DOT were not feasible due to geographic and staffing constraints. In 2007, a 37-year-old Chuuk resident was diagnosed with pulmonary TB, later confirmed as MDR TB. The patient lacked access to second-line drugs and died. Four additional MDR TB cases were identified by mid-2008, with three fatalities, including a 2-year-old child. In response to the high fatality rate and evidence of recent MDR TB transmission, FSM authorities requested CDC assistance in May 2008. An investigation identified two distinct MDR TB clusters in Chuuk, associated with different villages. The first cluster involved three cases with resistance to five drugs, while the second cluster involved two cases with resistance to three drugs. Household caregivers reported inconsistent or incomplete self-administered therapy among previous TB patients, contributing to the emergence of drug resistance. Contact investigations revealed 205 named contacts, 80% of whom were household members. Among these, three additional MDR TB cases were confirmed, including a 4-year-old who died of meningitis caused by MDR TB. Latent TB infection was diagnosed in 60% of contacts, with all household contacts receiving second-line drugs based on source case drug-susceptibility results. In response to the outbreaks, Chuuk implemented several measures, including procuring second-line drugs, establishing a dedicated TB ward, training staff in DOT and contact investigations, hiring outreach workers, and enhancing laboratory capacity. These efforts increased recorded TB incidence to 204 cases per 100,000 population in 2008. The emergence and transmission of MDR TB in Chuuk highlight the critical need for robust TB control practices, access to appropriate drugs, and laboratory capacity. Pediatric contacts are particularly vulnerable, and diagnosing and treating MDR TB in resource-limited settings remains challenging. The WHO global response plan for drug-resistant TB emphasizes strengthening public health infrastructure, improving surveillance, and enhancing management of drug-resistant cases to achieve global TB control goals. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), particularly carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP), pose a growing challenge in healthcare settings. The CDC and the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC) recommend aggressive infection control strategies, including contact precautions and adherence to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines for detecting carbapenemase production. Surveillance and early detection are critical to controlling CRE spread, especially in areas where CRE is endemic. The Modified Hodge Test (MHT) is a phenotypic test for detecting carbapenemase production in isolates with elevated but susceptible carbapenem MICs. Facilities should establish protocols for prompt notification of infection prevention staff when CRE is identified. Active surveillance cultures can identify undetected carriers and help prevent transmission. Enhanced infection control compliance, patient cohorting, and periodic prevalence surveys are essential for controlling CRE outbreaks. The emergence of CRE underscores the urgent need for improved detection and control strategies to address antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacteria. Early detection, strict infection control measures, and targeted surveillance can help limit the spread of these pathogens.
